I have never undertaken during the last five years of flux and change to speak with any degree of absolute certainty about anything connected with trade, for the situation has changed from day to day and from night to night. I can recall an order taken by a firm in Canada to be shipped to the United States; the goods were packed and when they reached Windsor to go across, the rate of duty owing to another classification had been so increased that it made it impossible to ship them without losing thousands of dollars. These things happen from day to day. I can only say that if we have adopted, as apparently we have, the principles laid down in the papers tabled to-day, we shall find it to be a very sorry day indeed for this Dominion of Canada. For I assure you, sir, that at any time before October it would have been possible to arrive at that arrangement, but I would not make it. I stand here to-night and say that I would not make it; I stand here to-night and say that I condemn it. I believe it to be bad, and I am as certain
(Mr. Bennett.]
as one can be in this changing world that the agreement which has been consummated will bring disaster to Canada.
I turn for a moment to the position in connection with the United States. I must say something in fairness to my colleagues and myself because in the twelve months ending December, 1935, Canada bought from the United States $28.83 per capita in Canadian money, and the United States bought from us $2.23. We had by constant and untiring effort reduced the commodity balance against Canada to the low sum of $34,000,000, at the end of December of last year. If you will allow for gold and silver that went to the United States as commodities you will find that at the end of 1935 there was a favourable balance for Canada of $60,000,000. That is a point of very great importance, and one of the reasons why today our dollar is at par or better; the reason lies in that changed trade balance. Under those circumstances and in view of what had been said we made proposals to the United States government as a basis for negotiations of which I do not believe you will find any similar record ip Canada. I am going to take the trouble to place it upon Hansard, because I believe it is desirable that the Canadian people should realize the basis upon which we were prepared to negotiate.
On November 14, 1934, the minister at Washington sent to the Secretary of State a dispatch which had been prepared with great care not by one man, nor by two, but by the joint effort of those in the permanent Canadian civil service, and had been considered by the* cabinet I believe on three occasions. It is as follows:
Sir, the government of Canada for many months have been giving careful consideration to the means whereby the exchange of commodities between Canada and the United States might be increased, and I have been instructed to present a statement of their views for the information of the government of the United States. The government of Canada believe that the time has come for definite action and that the declared desire of both governments to improve conditions of trade between the two countries should' now be carried into effect by the negotiation of a comprehensive trade agreement.
You will recall that when the Prime Minister of Canada visited Washington in April, 1933, at the invitation of the President of the United States, the development of trade between the two countries was sympathetically discussed. On April 29, 1933, Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Bennett issued a joint statement at the end of their conversations, which concluded as follows:
"We have also discussed1 the problems peculiar to the United States and Canada. We have agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between

The Address-Mr. Bennett
our two countries, and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent, but also the general improvement of world conditions."
At that time it was expected that at an early date the President would be vested with special powers to enter into agreements looking toward an increase in the exchange of commodities between the United States and other countries. Since Mr. Bennett's visit, informal discussions have been carried on, and several methods of improving trade relations between the two countries have been suggested and examined.
In the past eighteen months the governments of the United States and' Canada have repeatedly manifested their determination to increase international trade, by declarations of policy and by the conclusion of bilateral trade agreements.
Within that period of time Canada has made trade agreements with several European countries.
The policy of the Government of Canada with respect to trade relations with the United States was again stated by the Prime Minister of Canada speaking in the House of Commons on February 19, 1934. Mr. Bennett on that occasion referred to the fact that the governments of the United States and Canada had agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between the two countries and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent, but also a general improvement of world conditions, and indicated that the policy of the government was to continue their efforts to that end.
On July 21,	1933, at the international
Monetary and Economic Conference in London, the policy of the government of the United States was expressed by you in a resolution submitted on behalf of your government. This resolution declared that the governments represented at the conference should forthwith "initiate bilateral (or plurilateral) negotiations for the removal of prohibitions and restrictions and for the reduction of tariff rates; and declare that their aim in these treaties is substantial reduction of basic trade barriers, and not merely the removal of temporary and abnormal restrictions and increments imposed for bargaining purposes." The resolution continued: "In shaping its policy and in executing its obligations under any agreements, each government should direct its first and greatest efforts towards eliminating restrictions and reducing duties w-hich most clearly lack economic justification, particularly:
(a)	Duties or restrictions which not completely or almost completely exclude foreign competition, such as those which restrict importation of particular commodities to less than 5 per cent of the domestic consumption thereof;
(b)	Duties or restrictions on articles the imports of which have been substantially curtailed since 1929, as compared with domestic consumption;
(c)	Protective duties or restrictions which have been in effect a considerable period of time without bringing about a substantial domestic production of the protected commodities (say equal to 15 per cent of the total domestic consumption thereof)."
On December 16, 1933, on your motion, the Seventh International Conference of American
States at Montevideo adopted a resolution which declared that the Governments of the American Republics would promptly undertake "to promote trade among their respective peoples and other nations and to reduce high trade barriers through the negotiation of comprehensive bilateral reciprocity treaties based upon mutual concessions."
On February 22, 1934, the Department of State issued to the press a statement concerning trade negotiations with Canada, which reads as follows:
"The Trade between the United States and Canada is larger in normal times than that between any other two countries in the world, and it is natural that both countries should desire to restore the reciprocal flow of commodities to normal proportions. We hppe to be in a position at an early date to take steps looking to the conclusion of a trade agreement with Canada which will further the interests of both countries. We hope thus'to bring into practical application the 'good neighbour' policy between these two great countries which have so much in common." A few days later, on March 2nd, the President requested the Congress to enact legislation conferring on him authority to enter into trade agreements, in a message which concluded with the following words:
"I hope for early action. The many immediate situations in the field of international trade that to-day await our attention can be met effectively and with the least possible delay."
The legislation in question became law on June 12th. Since then your government has set up the organization necessary for the conduct of negotiations, carried on its preliminary investigations, initiated discussions with several governments, and proclaimed the conclusion of a trade agreement with Cuba. The objective of the United States in entering upon these negotiations was stated by you in a public address on November 1st to be "to break down all the artificial and excessive impediments put in the way of world commerce, not only in our own interests but for the benefit of all others as well, since only by restoring the -whole world can individual countries hope to remain economically healthy long."
It is hardly necessary to stress the importance to both the United States and Canada of their mutual trade. For many years each country has provided the other with either its largest or its second largest foreign market. From 1927 to 1932 and again in the first nine months of 1934, the total trade between Canada and the United States was greater than the total trade between the United States and any other country. In the last ten years, according to the figures of the Department of Commerce of the United States, the aggregate value of the trade between the two countries was more than ten billion dollars, and in the single year of 1929 it reached the great figure of $1,451 millions. During the decade ending in 1933 Canada provided a market for the products of the United States larger by one-fourth than the whole of Asia, about twice as large as Germany or all South America, nearly three times as large as France or Japan, nearly seven times as large as China, and more than ten times as large as the Soviet Union. In spite of the considerable decline in trade from the high level of 1929, Canada still provided a market in the first nine months of 1934 only slightly smaller than all Asia, nearly twice as large as all South America or Japan,
The Address-Mr. Bennett

between two and three times as large as Germany or France, four times as large as China, and twenty-two times as large as the Soviet Union. Over 30 per cent of all exports from Canada are currently sold in the United States, and notwithstanding the great difference in population of the two countries, about 15 per cent in value of all exports from the United States are currently sold in Canada. The relative importance of the market of each country ito the other, and the persistence of trading on a substantial scale throughout the changing phases of the business cycle, as revealed by the trade returns, demonstrate the inherent advantage of this interchange of commodities, and the tremendous potentialities of expansion under favourable conditions. But no useful purpose can be served by calculating the relative shares retained by each country in a total world trade that for four years has been steadily shrinking, until in 1933 it fell in value to approximately one-third of the level of 1929. If peace and prosperity are to be established on an enduring basis, it is essential to increase the absolute volume of world trade. No better beginning can be made than by taking steps to increase without delay the volume of trade between two countries which offer the most notable opportunity.
Recent trends in the balance of international payments emphasize the necessity of increasing the volume of trade between Canada and the United States. There are six major factors which chiefly determine the nature and extent of the current balance between the two countries. These are: (a) commodity trade; (b) interest and dividends; (c) freight payments; (d) tourist expenditures; (e) gold shipments, and (f) capital movements. On the first three items there has been for many years a heavy balance against Canada, which has been met by a favourable balance on tourist expenditures, by the shipment of gold, and by the movement of capital. An approximate annual balance between the two countries is normally achieved on such other items of international payments as insurance, advertising, royalties, and immigrant remittances, when these items are added together.
(a) Commodity Trade.
In no year since 1882 have Canadian exports to the United States exceeded in value Canadian imports from the United States. During the thirty years ending in 1933, Canada purchased in the United States almost 70 per cent of all her imports and sold in the United States only 37 per cent of all her exports. In the last decade, Canadians have spent over $1.60 in buying products of the United States for every dollar spent on Canadian products by purchasers in the United States. Canada has therefore been obliged to meet the debit balance thus arising by other means of payment. In the decade 1921 to 1930, according to the Department of Commerce of the United States, the balance payable by Canada to the United States on exchange of commodities averaged $287 millions a year. In 1932 and 1933-which were the acute years of the depression-the balance was more nearly equated; but in the first nine months of 1934 Canadian imports from the United States have increased more rapidly than Canadian exports to the United States, and the ratio between them currently stands at about 10:7.
[Mr. Bennett.!
(b)	Interest and Dividends.
The long-term investments in Canada of United States capital have been estimated at a total of about four billion dollars, offset by about one billion dollars of Canadian capital invested in the United States.
The interest paid annually by Canada to the United States in excess of the interest paid by the United States to Canada now amounts to about $125 millions, without taking into account instalments of principal payments, *which in recent years have averaged approximately $75 millions annually.
To this should be added an annual sum, amounting at present to between $25 and $50 millions, being the excess derived by the United States from dividends on investments in Canada over dividends from investments by Canada in the United States.
The United States investments in * securities issued or guaranteed by the dominion and provincial governments is estimated at $1,218 millions. During the depression there has been no default in the payment of interest or principal on any of those issues, even in face of the discount on the Canadian dollar which continued from the latter part of 1931 until late in 1933. Interest payments have been, of course, a continuing charge, the real burden of which has increased with the decline in prices. The strain on Canadian economy has been heavy, and it has only been borne by the adoption of special measures for the equalization of exports and imports.
Right there I will point out that that had to do with the very dumping and other measures to which I have referred. We can maintain our position for the equalization of exports and imports only by special measures. I continue:
(c)	Freight Charges.
Since the -war, net freight payments have been favourable to the United States to the extent of between $25 and $50 millions annually, and this substantial sum remains a debit item against Canada.
(d)	Tourist Expenditures.
The expenditures in Canada by visitors from the United States have been by far Canada's largest annual credit item. Canadian authorities estimate that the net balance on this account has been as high as $188 millions in one year, but since the depression the net Canadian surplus from this source has sharply declined, and amounted only to $60 millions in 1933.
If we adopt what Mr. Fielding felt he could not adopt, and what successive ministers of finance felt they could not adopt, namely, a provision to enable Canadians to bring back 8100 worth of goods from the United States', even twice a year, that item will disappear entirely so far as these favourable factors are concerned. It is estimated that not less than fifty or seventy-five million dollars worth of free goods will enter Canada and to all purposes will constitute a Canadian payment to the American union. I continue:

The Address-Mr. Bennett
(e)	Gold Shipments.
In some measure, Canada has been enabled to meet the adverse balance of payments through the development of the gold mining industry and the shipment in recent years of practically all the new-mined gold' to the United States. According to the figures of the Federal Reserve Board, the United States received a net balance on this account averaging $50 millions a year in the five years 19291933; in tile first eight months of 1934, gold valued at $64 millions at the new valuation was received from Canada, an amount practically equal to the Canadian gold production during the period. Production in Canada has increased substantially during the depression, and its value in the United States has been enhanced by the reduction in the gold content of the United States dollar. It is impossible, however, to expand production rapidly. Even if the entire Canadian production were shipped to the United States, it would still be insuffi-# cient by at least 25 millions annually to meet the net interest payments due in New York. Further, it may not be found possible to continue the shipment of the entire Canadian gold output to the United States.
In other words, we may require it here. I read;
(f)	Capital Movements.
It may be stated, in general terms, that in recent years the net Canadian credits from tourist expenditures and gold shipments have offset the net debits to the United States from interest, dividends, and freight, while the adverse Canadian balance on commodity trade has been met by the net movement of capital from the United States to Canada. Capital has moved both by new long-term investments in Canada and by the purchase of existing Canadian securities. In 1931 the flotation of new capital issues in New York virtually ceased, and the meeting of Canadian obligations in the United States became much more difficult; in fact, it was necessary in some instances to raise capital in Canada and transfer it to the United States to meet maturing obligations there. A reduction in imports therefore became urgently necessary if Canadian obligations were to be promptly and fully paid at maturity. The fall in commodity prices, the decline in Canadian exports to the United States, which was accentuated first by the United States Tariff Act of 1930 and' later by the imposition in 1932 of a 'heavy tax on imported lumber, the discount against the Canadian dollar, and the heavy falling off in tourist expenditures, combined to make the situation still more difficult. Most of the factors responsible for this difficult situation still persist.
There has been a lessening of the movement of capital from the United States, and one of the reasons is the very one I referred to in connection with the Ontario situation. In fact, it is well known that the representations made by those who represented investments in this country of substantial sums of money, evidenced by securities which they had distributed over every part of the American union, are having a very considerable
effect upon the willingness to bring further capital into this country. I continue:
Since the beginning of the depression, amongst countries heavily indebted to the United States, Canada stands almost alone in having promptly discharged in full its obligations payable in the United States. If this record is to be maintained, it is clear, in view, of the uncertainty as to international capital movements, that the exports of Canadian goods to the United States must be increased or the imports of goods from the United States into Canada decreased.
It should be realized that certain formidable obstacles to the lowering of tariff barriers now prevailing in other parts of the world are not present between the United States and Canada. The opportunities of a new continent have resulted in a parallel economic and social development almost without precedent. Standards of living and' working conditions are similar on both sides of the international boundary. The measures of protection which each government has imposed against the products of the other country have not been determined by a desire to exclude the products of cheap labour. In these difficult times, countries seeking to maintain high domestic standards of living have a common interest in expanding trade with each other. For the past year, also, the Canadian dollar has been close to parity with the United States dollar, and the disturbing effects of exchange instability have in large part disappeared. Even if the desired general revival of international trade should still be delayed for a considerable period, there is much to be said in favour of an immediate attempt to increase the volume of commerce between these two neighbouring countries, whose traditions and ideals of social and economic progress are so alike.
As I pointed out a moment ago, and as I repeat again, we were able through the efforts we made to reduce the adverse balance against Canada in commodities to $34,000,000 at the end of December, 1935, and after creating $95,000,000 of gold, there was a balance in our favour of about $60,000,000. I continue:
Attention has been directed to the trade agreements between Canada and the other members of the British Commonwealth of Nations signed in Ottawa in 1932. In some quarters the statement has been made that these agreements render difficult the negotiations of a comprehensive and effective trade agreement between Canada and the United States. An examination of the facts will demonstrate conclusively that such is not the case. The agreements concluded at Ottawa in 1932 have been of immense importance in increasing the trade between the several Nations of the British Commonwealth. The market of the United Kingdom in particular has been a most valuable outlet for Canadian products. In return for the market thus assured Canada has continued and enlarged the preferences which had been accorded the United Kingdom since 1897. The Ottawa agreements do not, however, preclude and in fact have not precluded the signatories from offering extensive and valuable tariff concessions to other countries, and it may be stated positively that
The Address-Mr. Bennett

the government of Canada is free to enter into an agreement with the United States covering a wide range of products.
The government of Canada is prepared to join the government of the United States in a declaration that their common objective is the attainment of the freest possible exchange of natural products between the two countries. It is recognized that this objective cannot be attained in the immediate future, as important interests in both countries would be disturbed unduly by the sudden removal of existing tariffs on all natural products. The government of Canada would therefore favour, as the first step, the reductions included in the proposals set out in the next paragraph, to be succeeded by progressive mutual reductions in the duties on natural products, leading to the attainment of the declared objective.
I am authorized to put forward the following outline as a suitable basis for the negotiation of a trade agreement:	_	_
(a)	A mutual undertaking to maintain during the lifetime of the agreement the unrestricted free entry of commodities now on the free list of either country.
(b)	The mutual concession of tariff treatment as favourable as that accorded to any other foreign country; this means that Canada would extend to the United States its intermediate tariff involving reductions from the present rates of duty on some 700 items, including both natural and manufactured products, together with a number of further reductions below the intermediate tariff rates through the extension to the United States of concessions made by Canada in trade conventions with foreign countries.
(c)	The reduction by 50 per cent of the existing United States rates of duty, as authorized by the Tariff Act of 1034. on a specified number of natural products, including inter alia, lumber, fish, potatoes, milk and cream, and live cattle; a number of other agricultural products, and several minerals both metallic and non-metallic.
(d)	The reduction of the existing rates of duty by the United States on a number of partly or wholly manufactured products of Canada, including some processed natural products and certain products in which hydroelectric power comprises an important element in the cost of production.
(e)	The reduction of the existing rates of duty by Canada on a number of natural and partly or wholly manufactured products of the United States.
In view of the declared policy of the governments of the United States and Canada to improve existing trade relations, and of the progress already made in both countries in the necessary preparatory studies, there would appear to be no barrier to the immediate initiation of negotiations and their speedy conclusion. I am desired, therefore, to request that I may be furnished with a statement of the views of the government of the United States on this highly important question.
I have the honour to be, with the highest consideration, Sir,
Your most obedient, humble servant, (Sgd.) W. D. Herridge The Hon. Cordell Hull,
Secretary of State of the United States, Washington, D.C.
fMr. Bennett.]
I want to point out, sir, that I place that upon the records of Hansard in order that it may be there.

speechtext: What is the date?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext:
I gave the date; it is November, 1934. I place it on Hansard because it furnishes the basis of the negotiations that were carried on by the last administration. We did not promise to give them anything nor did they promise to give us anything, but we did say, "Here is the basis for negotiations"; and when we found-and I want to make this abundantly clear-that we could not secure what we believed to be only a very moderate compensation for what we [DOT] were asked to give, we declined to give it. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. We had settled questions of lumber; we had settled many other questions; but do you suppose for a single moment that any government in Canada is justified in giving the favoured nation treatment and the intermediate rates to the United States without the entry into their market of Canadian fish from the Atlantic coast? Does anyone suggest that we are justified in doing that? And yet that is what has been done, except as regards skates, and, I think, one other brand of fish.
Take agricultural products; take dairy products; look at the rates of duty provided for in the agreement, and we will discuss them item by item when they come before the house. I want to make clear only one thing, namely, that for what we could get we were not prepared to give what was asked. That is the story, stated in that simple sentence; and that is the reason I have read this, so that there might be no misunderstanding as to the basis of the negotiations on the broadest possible foundation, comprising everything. We were not prepared to see every treaty we made with twenty-three countries enuring to the benefit of the United States unless we obtained a quid pro quo that was worth while.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott), in the speeches delivered during the campaign, said that the President of the United States would not negotiate with the Bennett government, and the Prime Minister of this country said that he would negotiate a treaty in ninety days. Does that mean that they had an arrangement that no agreement was to be made with that government, or does it mean this-

speechtext: And I say, "Shame."

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext:
The shame lies with the Postmaster General and the Prime Minister, as I am going to show, who went round the country making these statements. He said, "Put me in office and I will negotiate it in ninety days"; and the Postmaster General said, "Mr. Roosevelt will not make a treaty or a bargain with Mr. Bennett." That is what he said, as reported in the journals of the country. I ask this question:	Did he
make that statement by reason of having any arrangement with the United States government or anyone connected with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext:
If he answers no, then why did he make it? Is that fair political warfare, to have the people of the country believe he had an arrangement whereby, if he came into office, he could negotiate an agreement in ninety days? He did it in much less time, as I shall point out. The Postmaster General said, "We can do this, but he will not enter into a bargain with Bennett." Well, let me point out that during all that time the government of the United States was urging that, even though an election was pending, we should carry on our negotiations; and I decline to believe that the government of the United States was a party to any arrangement that would reflect upon itself. I say, shame; I agree with the Prime Minister; but the shame is to those who went about the country and tried to induce the people to believe that the United States would not carry on negotiations with the Conservative government of the day, but that there had to be a change of government to make a bargain with the United States. That is what I say.
I want to make it clear that under no circumstances was the late government prepared to enter into the agreement in question. 1 was not prepared to sacrifice Canadian ports; I was not prepared to sacrifice Canadian fishermen ; I was not prepared to sacrifice the dairy products of the country to the manufacturing interests of the United States, and I am not now, nor do I believe the Canadian people are. I have it at least from one man, an ex-member of parliament,-well, one should
not quote men without names, so that we will leave that by the way. What is thought of it by persons, by newspapers in the United States or in Canada, is not the issue. There are in this agreement many things which represent arrangements arrived at necessarily by the late government; for no government could negotiate an agreement in forty-eight hours. There are may items that are advantageous to the United States and to Canada; there are mutual benefits, mutual advantages; there are provisions that are helpful to Canada and to the United States. But you have to decide on balance, and the government with which I was associated decided, on balance, that we could not make that bargain. I will not go into details-magazines, manufactured products, the effect upon the income of the railroads of the country, fruit and vegetables. Already in western Canada commercial representatives of the manufacturing houses of the central west are offering their wares, prepared to pay the duty at the reduced rate, because the freight rate from central United States into western Canada is only one-third what it is from eastern Canada.
There you have again the old story of the struggle between east and west and north and south, the question whether we shall succeed in developing a Canada or not. Are the fishermen on the Atlantic to be sacrificed along with the dairy producer, the vegetable producer, and all these others that we will take up in detail when the schedule is before the house? On balance, I say, I was not prepared to ask that the government of Canada should agree to any such bargain. The favoured nation treatment and six or seven hundred items of the intermediate tariff were matters of such gigantic importance to the United States that I felt they should pay and pay handsomely before they got. such an advantage; and if they got it without paying handsomely, it would be sacrificing the interests of Canada to a mere chimera, I was not prepared to do this, because on balance this bargain is against my country. It is against Canada; it is against its development, against its economic integrity, against its future, against everything we have builded all these years, the thing we have toiled and sacrificed to create. And I am sure that hon. members within sound of my voice will have reason to realize how true that is if they take these items schedule by schedule, item by item, studying every phase of the subject.
An agreement thus arrived at-fancy! Just a few hours and it is all over. My objection to Liberal policies in this country has been and is to-day that, unfortunately, they are
The Address-Mr. Bennett

concerned with the event of the d)ay and not with the implications of their acts. I could give two or three illustrations, but I will not do so at length. One is the railroad situation. A third transcontinental came into being under circumstances that brought great glory for the moment, loud cheers, and a vast expenditure of public money. Look at the record and see the amendments proposed by Sir Robert, then Mr. Borden. The implications were not considered; he dealt with the implications; they considered to-day; that is all. Sufficient unto the evil- is the day thereof. Take the western provinces-

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: Sufficient unto the day-

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext:
I put it, in this instance, the right way, not the way it is put in Scripture.
Now let me go a step further. I will give you a second illustration. What about our western provinces? In 1905 they came into being, and they were given a grant of money in lieu of their resources. Now look at the statute. I remember one who appeared at this interprovincial conference not Long since, who said, "What do we owe to posterity? What we need is money." The immediate moment! And yet hardly had they come into being than day after day they began to feel crippled by not having their resources, and agitations were carried forward just as I pointed out they would be, that one day they must get the-ir resources. What happened? They gave over to the provinces -their natural resources in their entirety, with their subsidies as well, so that other provinces of confederation claimed that they had not been fairly dealt with; and the province of British Columbia received an interim grant of $750,000 to bring it -to something like the same position as the -other provinces. Not -content with that, for the immediate moment, for the election moment, $4,000,000 was paid to Manitoba for the purpose oif putting it -on an equality with other provinces of the confederation. And then, not only were Saskatchewan and Alberta given their resources, and money in lieu of them; they were given a reference to an arbitration to decide how much they should get for the -time when they did not -have them, but during which they had the money. They got an award in their favour. Then you had the province of British Colu-mibia complaining and you had the -provinces by the sea complaining, and not improperly, because the government of the day had not considered the implications of their act. They were content with the choice o-f the day, -the spoils of the day, in the way in which it brought 
strength and power for the moment in a general election. But the implications are there.
Here is a treaty, a trade agreement made in a few hours. They say: We were going to finish it in ninety days, and we did it in a few days. The very references of the Prime Minister are not to the terms of -the agreement, but: We have been in office only a few days and look at what we have done; we have signed a .trade agreement. The mere signing of the trade agreement w-as not a matter of importance. The matter of importance is; Was the agreement in its implications favourable to the Dominion of Canada? It is not pride in having done something in a day, or in having done something in an hour. A child may destroy in a minu-te a most complex piece of machinery, a watch that might take a man a week to build. Do you pat the child on the back because he can destroy the watch w-ith a single stroke? He does not think of the implications of -his act. Here we have a trade -agreement, unbalanced, as I have endeavoured to show, highly detrimental to the highest interests of this dominion. Not only will i-t be found to be distrastrous in its operations, but it sows seeds of discord instead of promoting harmony in this dominion. Here you are, with great channels of trade that were bui-llt with such effort. I think of the taxes people have borne to establish channels of trade, east and west, but now we are going to supply these wants with a cheap rate from the western United States, where the big factories are, ,to western Canada, and we can look in vain for traffic. That is one side of the picture.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether hon. members realize how difficult it is for one, who as the head of a government might get some credit for negotiating an agreement which the other party was willing and ready to make, so far as I can ascertain from the statements made, not to do it, even though an election were pending, because he felt he dare not do it and be fair to the country in which he was born. I will admit that it is a nice thing to have the duty on- lumber cut in two. Of course it is. I will admit it is a good thing to be able to sell Scotch whiskey four years old at a lower rate of duty. This will increase our trade balance for the moment. I will admit all that. But when I think of the fisherman who is not allowed to compete with the trawlers of Gloucester except on a basis that amounts to prohibition, although they both fish on the Grand Banks of the Atlantic ocean; when I think of the dairy producers in this country, unable to sell their cream, milk, or butter except on a basis of eight cents a pound

The Address-Mr. Bennett
duty to be overcome, eight cents of prohibition, as everyone knows; when I think of many, many other items that I might mention to this house now, but that- it would be undesirable to do, perhaps, in view of the discussion that must take place, I can only say that on balance this treaty is disastrous to Canada.-
On one point I mentioned, about magazines, I have a strong feeling, because of those unconscious influences that mould the character of a nation, that make the character of a people. We had to some extent stopped their sale; it had been reduced by one-half. The revenues had been added to by this duty where the advertising was more than; 20 per cent. The standard of our magazines had been improved; the price had been reduced. We were getting a national consciousness. Who, listening to a broadcast, does not realize that there too is an unconscious influence that makes for a national character? What a difficult time, sir, in endeavouring to build up a nation! Yet, with one, just one stroke of the pen, after a few hours' consideration, all this is forgotten; the long struggles to maintain relations between east and west over that dismal area north of lake Superior are all forgotten. Now watch the progress. All you have to do is to read the speech of Mr. Hull, Secretary of State of the United States, on that point, and you have no difficulty.
I will not now deal with the effect upon our industrial life of the Japanese arrangement; I will do that also later.
As to the railway problem, I do not propose to say more than- this: it is quite clear to me that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe) has not grasped1 the provisions of the act under which the trustees operate; if he had, he certainly would' not have' made the speech he did. It is an elementary rule that when a private corporation engaged in the operation of railways does not meet its bond interest, applications are made to the board to appoint a receiver; the receiver no longer pays interest on the bonds, nor dividends; he accumulates the money for the purpose of bettering the financial structure, and then in due time a reorganization may take place. Now, the Dominion of Canada was behind the bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway; it had endorsed its guarantee upon them, and the provinces had done likewise. I wonder how many hon. members realize that if the provinces of Canada had to pay their guarantees that we now have accepted, those who had guaranteed in the west would be entirely bankrupt. We are paying the entire guarantee in British
Columbia on the Canadian Northern. We are paying the entire guarantees on the Grand Trunk, Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In Nova Scotia we are paying on the Halifax and Southwestern, and in New Brunswick we are paying on the section that runs through the centre of that province. How many have paused to realize what that means to the taxpayers of this country? When we were confronted with that situation, Mr., now Sir Edward Beatty, and the late Sir Henry Thornton thought it desirable that a commission should be appointed1 to investigate thesie matters, to investigate what might be done on the one hand to save from' receivership the one privately owned road, and on the other to reduce the operating losses, the national losses I should say. This commission that was appointed, comprising as it did1 the ablest men available, presided over by the present chief justice of Canada, with Lord Ashfield, who was the leading authority upon transportation in Great Britain, went west.
When they made their first trip west they realized that the amalgamation of these roads, in the sense in which that term was used, was an impossible thing, and they advised methods / and means whereby there would be the benefits of receivership from the standpoint of the properties themselves and, on the other hand, the closest possible relation between the government and the operation as far as finding capital was concerned. Had it been a private enterprise and that private enterprise had defaulted, the sale by the receiver of receiver's certificates would have provided the necessary money to run the road. So year by year the trustees asked this government or whatever government might be in power to find for them the money that otherwise would be found through receiver's certificates to enable ihe road to function until such time as conditions improved.
Naturally the one great object this commission had in mind was to divorce the operation of the railways from politics, not politics in the narrow sense but politics in the broad sense, to divorce the road from the pressure, as the situation was put by one of the English members of this commission, that is exerted for the purpose of inducing railways to yield to communities for special reasons, a branch line here and a branch line there, the pressure of a member here and of a member there. All these things were to be overcome by the appointment of a small commission that would take the place of any receiver on the one hand and be free from the exercise of political control and pressure on the other.
The Address-Mr. Bennett

I think the minister has misunderstood the purpose of the act. That was the purpose. He is now going to modify and change that into some other system, one similar to that condemned by the commission. They said that it was no longer possible to operate successfully under the conditions that then obtained. I am not going to do more than await the legislation, making this short statement because I do not believe the minister has thoroughly appreciated and understood what has been said.
Then with respect to the creation of parliamentary secretaries, there is nothing new in that; it was done here once before. We had parliamentary secretaries here in this country, in this parliament. When Sir Robert Borden asked Sir George Murray to come here and make a report, he did so; he reported in favour of parliamentary secretaries and they were appointed. I recall this very vividly, and I recall the result. Somehow in this country, under the conditions that exist, it will foe found that they will not function successfully. That is the experience of the past and I do not think times have changed in that regard. I wish it were otherwise, because personally I favoured such a system at that time and I favour it now if it were possible to make it work out successfully, but I am afraid it will not for reasons that are known to many members and that must be known to those who have studied conditions as they existed at the time it was tried.
I congratulate the Prime Minister and the government upon the consolidation of departments. With all deference I suggest to the government that the Department of Transportation had better be called the Department of Communications because it will deal not only with transport but also with broadcasting and wireless communications. The bill I had drafted contemplated the creation of a department of communications and that that department should deal with railways and canals, marine, radio, wireless and certain features of post office work that, as hon. gentlemen know, now come from abroad to that department in connection with broadcasting and communication of that kind.

I was coming to [DOT] that.
The other matter we thought should be dealt with by that minister was civil aviation, and in the bill I prepared I suggested the name should be the Department of Communications as being more in keeping with the functions the department would discharge. Any knowledge I have is available

to the government should they desire to make use of it. I congratulate the minister on having given effect to that at once, because I say to him and to this house that if he had not done it at once he could not have done it at all. I learned by experience, in my effort to do it, that it would be possible to carry out that plan only immediately after an election. For the same reason I congratulate the minister on having dealt with the harbour commissions as he has. During my unsuccessful efforts to deal with that question in that way I realized that the only method by which it could be dealt with was to do it right away, at once. Then it is an accomplished fact, and as an accomplished fact it is res ipsa loquitur. At any rate I do congratulate the government and I assure them that in my judgment at least they have accomplished a very much needed reform. I believe the country will be the better for the consolidation of these services,
I may tell my hon. friends that the order in council had been drafted consolidating Interior, Mines, Immigration and Soldier Settlement in one department. From the information I received and which we all obtained, it was believed that the Department of Labour might deal with one branch I have named with more effect than could any other department, but at the time of dissolution we had arrived at no conclusion as to how the departments could be best divided in the public interest. At any rate this is a step in the right direction and in my judgment cannot but be useful.
I think the reference to the reduction in the number of ministers is hardly in keeping with the rest of the speech from the throne, for at the time the ministers without portfolio were appointed it was known that a reconstruction of the government would take place after the election.

just for election purposes?

speechtext:
No, not for election
purposes but for the purpose of making it clear that they were men of capacity who would be available when the time arrived. It was for the same purpose, I take it, that the right hon. gentleman had recourse to somewhat similar methods on previous occasions.
There is one other matter about which I should like to speak, even though I may trespass unduly upon the time of the house. There is some fear being manifested in many quarters with regard to the administration of justice. The heated debate that took place in this chamber in consequence of the

The Address-Mr. Bennett
Regina riots is not beyond the memory of many who sit here to-night. Then, after that, certain legal proceedings were taken and certain men were sent up for trial, with a preliminary hearing before a magistrate. In the meantime one of them, Mr. Evans, and others met together and concluded that they would petition the premier of Saskatchewan, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). So local citizens' defence committees sent out requests that each man should sign a petition to the hon. gentleman saying:
I have been circularized by the Citizens' Defence Committee, of Regina, acting on behalf of the 38 arrested relief camp strikers now incarcerated in the Regina jail, on charges arising out of rioting at Regina, July 1st, to impress upon you the need for the immediate setting up by your government of a representative commission to investigate and place the blame for that affair.
I do not concur with the citizens' committee of Regina on the above, nor on their further proposal, that any and all trials on charges arising out of the Regina riots should be postponed, pending the findings of the above mentioned commission.
That was widely circulated by this citizens' legal defence committee, which made striking charges against Mr. Guthrie, Minister of Justice at that time, and myself. The result was that after the defeat of the late government the provincial government at Regina set up a commission consisting of three judges, though our Judges Act does make reference to the fact that the dominion, having paid their salaries, has something to say about the matter.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: They were set up the day after the riots.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: Yes, they were set up but they did not function until later. Now what has taken place? I have been in western Canada; for some time lately there has been a great deal of concern among thoughtful people-not the vocal people-as to what all this means. Here are three judges holding an investigation into a matter that has been referred in part to the courts. There is no reason why any province should not hold an investigation if its sees fit as to how its officers have discharged their duties or how other work has been done within the ambit of their powers. Chief Justice Brown refused to permit evidence to be given as to where the $500 came from that Evans received, and that is quite a substantial sum of money.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: To some people.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER

Yes, to all of us. He refused to permit that to be gone into. But this strange thing has happened; there has been 12739-5
called into that box a man, one of these trekkers, and he has sworn that he saw a mounted policeman smashing the head of Miller, who died. This is not a trial. Now what sort of trial are you going to have? Did you ever hear of an investigation of that kind while trials were pending? I can understand an investigation wdth respect to the circumstances leading up to it or with respect to it. Mr. Evans was in Calgary while this commission is still sitting, and it now threatens to go to British Columbia and Alberta to investigate matters that certainly are outside the province of Saskatchewan and beyond the commission's powers. It has now been sitting for many days; the whole morale of the police has been visibly affected, and the sentiment is abroad that justice is becoming political, which is a terrible thing. It is something I hoped we would never have happen in this country.
In that connection there is another matter to which I must refer, of which I read in the press of Ontario. Only a few days ago there appeared a report that the Minister of Justice had referred to the court of appeal the question whether a new trial should not be granted with respect to a matter that had been disposed of in 1925, I think, or thereabouts. There is one thing that I think we should be able to say, namely, that there is finality about justice in this country. This case has been before successive ministers of justice; it was made an issue in a provincial election and much talked about, but in the report made by the Department of Justice while the present minister was the minister, it was stated that any interference would be "a lamentable miscarriage of justice." Certainly the last Minister of Justice arrived at that conclusion, and certainly with my trifling knowledge of law I was wholly of his opinion. It does seem to me that to have in various provinces of this dominion the impression that there is uncertainty-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me to interrupt? Does he think it is right to discuss this matter when *it is before the court of appeal of Ontario and when on that account I cannot very well speak of the matters which forced the decision which was reached?

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext:
The hon. gentlemen who applaud most loudly are of course least familiar with this matter. The Minister of Justice doubtless heard me say this afternoon that matters which are sub judice I do not desire to discuss. There are a great many

The Address-Mr. Bennett

things I would say if I did so desire. I have not even mentioned names; I have not discussed the merits of the case; I have discussed the principle of a reference being made by the minister, which is all I can do now. It is now before the court; what the court may or may not do, I am not going to discuss at the moment, but after the court has given its decision I think a discussion may be very desirable, in fact may be absolutely essential in the public interest. That is all I have to say with respect to that matter.
There remains one other matter that I cannot pass without some short reference, and that is the allegation made by the Prime Minister that I endeavoured to deprive or succeeded in depriving Mr. Vincent Massey of his position as minister at Washington. I refer to this with great regret; I do so not only with regret but with something akin to sorrow, be -ause I cannot think the Prime Minister co tld possibly have appreciated his own position when he made the statement he did. According to the report in the Ottawa Citizen, at Winnipeg on October 11, 1935, Mr. King told an audience that after the Conservatives took office in 1930 Vincent Massey had been recalled from Washington in order that a relative of the Prime Minister could be sent to keep Mr. Bennett in the limelight. That is the statement as repeated in the press. Speaking in Toronto a few nights later I ventured to think that possibly the Prime Minister had confused Washington with London, because of what I shall presently say. But at Montreal the Prime Minister made the following statement:
Another of Mr. Bennett's statements was a demand for withdrawal of Mr. King's charge that Hon. Vincent Massey had been recalled from Washington in order that a relative of Mr. Bennett's might be appointed'.
"The statement I made in Winnipeg I repeat to-night as absolutely true," Mr. King declared.
Now even though it may take a little time I have to read the order in council which was passed on July 24, 1930, by the government of the present Prime Minister. Here it is, P.C. 1684, and it reads as follows:
The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, advise that the Honourable Vincent Massey, a member of His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada, be appointed High Commissioner for Canada in London from the 23rd July, 1930, under the act, chapter 92 of the Revised Statutes of 1927, in succession to the Honourable Peter C. Larkin, deceased; and that his duties include supervision over the various agencies of the Canadian government in the United Kingdom as described in the order in council (P.C. 330, 10th Eebruary, 1922) by which Mr. Larkin was appointed.
The committee, on the same recommendation, further advise that His Majesty the King in 
respect of Canada be humbly moved to issue Mr. Massey's letter of recall from the United States, and to indicate that Mr. Massey has fulfilled his mission to the entire satisfaction of His Majesty in respect of Canada.
"Fulfilled his mission." Could anything be clearer. That was on July 24, 1930, 'and the government. of which I was the head came into being on August 7 of the same year. But in the meantime correspondence 'had taken place between Mr. Massey and myself. He came to Ottawa and he represented himself to be the Canadian high commissioner at London. I saw him, heard his story, and he wrote me this letter:
Batterwood House Near Port Hope, Ontario
August 14, 1930
My dear Prime Minister:
I appreciate your courtesy in arranging our conversation of yesterday in answer to my letter requesting an expression of your wishes concerning my appointment to the high com-missionership in London.
I left the legation at Washington and accepted a transfer to London on the understanding that the office of high commissioner was an integral part of our service abroad differing, of course, in its procedure from our foreign diplomatic offices but akin to these in the qualifications of its personnel and in the relation of that personnel to the government which it serves. I now realize that our ideas regarding this are at variance. In our discussion on this subject you were good enough to make clear your view that the office of high commissioner should be held by someone in close political association with the government of the day, and I understood from what you said that you had in mind plans for this post as a result of which my own appointment could no longer stand.
In these circumstances I, of course, at once offered you my resignation from the high commissionership which I now confirm-the resignation to take effect whenever you so desire.
In, resigning from this post in our service abroad, of which I have been a member for three and a half years, I should like to say that no one belonging to the service and who has been engaged in its work, could retire from a post in it without a feeling of having been greatly privileged.
With kind regards.
Yours sincerely, Vincent Massey.
The Hon. R. B. Bennett, P.C., K.C.,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa, Ontario.
He told me he was going hunting, and I did not answer him until September 16, 1930, at which time I sent the following letter:
Dear Mr. Massey:-
I acknowledge the receipt of your communication of August 14th, and express my regret that absence from Ottawa for a period of nearly two weeks and great pressure of work since my return have prevented an earlier reply. I also recall that you did not expect to return from your hunting trip until this week.

The Address-Mr. Bennett
During our interview on Augsut 13th, I informed you that the present Conservative government considered it proper to adhere to the spirit of the statute creating the office of High Commissioner for Canada in Great Britain, and to affirm the policy which has developed under it, by appointing as its representative one who through conviction could fully subscribe to the declared views of the government relating to the conduct of the affairs of this country in Great Britain; and that any departure from that principle could only be justified on the ground of the more effective prosecution of the policies which this government believes should, in the interests of Canada, be maintained and developed.
As it was agreed that you could not personally approve these policies, it therefore followed, in my opinion at least, that they should more properly be entrusted to one who sincerely believed in their effectiveness.
For this reason it has been determined to accept your resignation as High Commissioner for Canada in Great Britain, and in so doing I would ask you to receive the expression of my belief in the high service you have for some years rendered Canada in a position, which from many points of view cannot, as you suggest, be regarded as in purpose essentially similar to the one you now resign.
I may observe that you are in error in assuming that you were transferred from the position of minister at Washington to that of High Commissioner at London. The order in council distinctly appointed you High Commissioner under the provisions of a Canadian statute, and is also the authority for directing that application should be made to His Majesty for your letter of recall as Minister to the United States. Such letter of recall is actually dated the 5th of August last.
Yours faithfully,
R. B. Bennett.
The Auditor General's report shows that Mr. Massey drew his salary as minister to Washington until' July 22, and' that he drew his salary as high commissioner to Great Britain until the day he was relieved, through the acoeptanoe of his resignation.
In order that there may be no misunderstanding and because the exact dates of these occurrences become perhaps of some importance, I believe I should give those dates. I find that Mr. Herridge was appointed to the position on March 7, 1931, and1 I believe that information makes the record complete.
I regret having to make these observations this evening, but in view of the certainty with which the right hon. gentleman spoke it does seem somewhat difficult to understand why he should have persisted in it. I turn to the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1931, Volume II, Part E, page 6 dealing with vote-credit 240, Canadian representation at Washington. Under this heading it is shown that the Hon. Vincent Massey, at $12,000 salary, drew from April 1 to July 22, $3,709.68. Then, on the previous
page under vote-credit 239, high commissioner's office, we find that from July 23 to September 16, at the rate of $12,000 he received $1,823.65. Incidentally, his moving expenses were paid, the cheque being issued for that after the termination of his arrangements with our government. He had moved his furniture before the date in August on which he saw me in Ottawa. I mention that because I hope the right hon. gentleman will realize there was an error and that we had nothing at all to do with displacing Mr. Massey. He vacated that post, and the present Prime Minister had asked His Majesty the late King to signify his pleasure, on the basis of Mr. Massey having fulfilled his duty. Of course a recall letter is never presented until the new minister takes his place. The minister may have died, or he may have filled a dozen other offices, or he may have gone to St. Petersburg. The actual presentation of the letter takes place when the new man steps in, as was done here when Mr. MacNider was succeeded, and as was done even more recently, in the case of the United States. I mention this matter in order that there may be no misapprehension with respect to what might be thought to be, shall I say, an effort on the part of the leader of the late government to dispose of the services of Mr. Massey at Washington.
There is one other matter about which I should like to speak, one which is personal in a sense. The criticism was that the negotiation of that agreement should have extended over a long time. Again I say that my right hon. friend had five years in which to negotiate an agreement with the United States. If I had waited five years there would be no agreement at this time or any time to come. My right hon. friend made it extremely difficult for the incoming government to make the agreement by putting off so long dissolving parliament, by holding on to office two years, at least, beyond the time he should have continued having regard to the views of the people of this country, and bringing matters to the point where it was difficult, within the limited time that remained to the government of the United States before it would again have to appeal to the country, to attempt the negotiation of a trade agreement such as the one that has been put through. I just wish at the moment to point out to my right hon. friend, seeing that he knows a little of the importance of doing some things at one time if they are to be done at all, that the making of an agreement with the United States and Canada in the matter of trade was one of the most urgent matters a government could be confronted with, and if the moment had not been seized, and seized to the full by the government itself, it would, I believe, have been impossible at this time to effect any agreement with the United States.

Press. Doctor Dafoe said that years ago, in the old parliaments, the blue ribbon of the legal profession was generally given that man, or he was regarded as having earned it, who had won a foremost place in his profession and then won as well a seat in parliament. I think I may truly say that by the speech he delivered to-day, the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) has already won the blue ribbon not of his profession only but also of parliament. He brings as an invaluable acquisition to this House of Commons the great abilities and talents which have become so evident to all in his profession, and indeed to the country generally, not only by the leading role he has so long played in the courts, but equally by the outstanding place he holds on the platform in the province from which he comes.
May I also congratulate very warmly my young friend the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemount (Mr. Fournier), who has charmed and delighted us all with his brilliant address in French, and in part in English as well. My friend was selected for this responsible duty as the youngest member on the Liberal side of the house. He has had some experience in business, but has given up business to enter one of the learned professions. He is now, I believe, engaged in studies at the university preparing himself for the practice of law. I think I may say to my hon. friend that, if he conserves his health and strength and continues with industry as he has done, he will achieve a very high place both in his profession and in the public life of our country. I extend to him not only my congratulations but my best wishes as well.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of joining with the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and with the mover (Mt. Slaght) and seconder (Mr. Fournier) of the resolution for an address to His Excellency, in saying how delighted we all are that His Excellency Lord Tweeds-muir has been chiosen to be the king's representative in this country. The fact that Lord Tweedsmuir had the close personal association he enjoyed with the late King George, that he had the honour of writing of the life and reign of the king as he has done so charmingly and effectively in The King's Grace,-and that he represented his late majesty as commissioner to the assembly of the Church of Scotland-all these associations with the late king, whose appointee he was, are additional links with himself which are much cherished by the people of this country. The warm welcome which has been extended to Lord
Tweedsmuir since his arrival in Canada speaks for itself. It has made clear to him, I am sure, that his great achievements and his versatile gifts have been well known to the people of Canada for many years. We all appreciate his excellency's expression of pleasure at the association to which he is looking forward for the next five years. It is an association, with both himself and the Lady Tweedsmuir, to which the people of Canada of all classes and in oil parts are also looking forward with great- pleasure.
Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, as was natural enough, has sought to bolster up the position of his small army and himself by saying that a great many of the members on this side of the house were returned by a minority of votes. He sought in those words to create the impression that, perhaps, after all, we who are so numerous on this side do not represent to the extent that we appear to do, the people of Canada. May I say that, had it not been for candidates returned by a minority of the votes, there would have hardly been any one on the other side of the house at all, and our numbers would have been very much larger than they are. Let me give a figure or two in regard to the situation. We have on this side of the house 178 Liberal members. When I speak of this side of the house of course I include the best of the other side. In that regard I must apologize for having failed to mention that, when my right hon. friend was congratulating those who moved and seconded the address at the time he had a large following immediately behind him on this side, he said they were most deserving of congratulation because of what they represented of the feelings of the people of Canada towards his government. Well, if that was the case, what must my right hon. friend think of the extent of the congratulations which should be conveyed to the mover and seconder today, when he finds himself encompassed by the cloud of witnesses which surround him telling of what the people think respectively of him and of me? I am putting it in this personal way in order to keep company with my right hon. friend-what I should say, speaking to the house and the country, is what they thought of the respective policies of the different parties as enunciated by their respective leaders. There are 178 Liberal members. It is true that of that number 85 were returned by a minority of votes. But may I point out-and it was something which was stressed over and over again by myself and other Liberal speakers in the campaign

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
that one of the unavoidable effects of a large number of parties in a campaign is that candidates are bound to be returned in increasing numbers by a minority of votes. There has never been a campaign in Canada in which there were so many parties contesting the honours as we had in the last election. In addition to the old Conservative party, we had our friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We had the new revolutionary army, the Reconstruction party; and we had our friends who came into being as a federal party after the election had been called, and who were fortunate in getting in at that particular moment, running for the first time as Social Creditors. Furthermore, we had some independent members. Altogether it was a great array. But the mere fact' that there were so many candidates made it inevitable that a very large number of members of parliament would be returned by a minority of votes. It so happens that eighty-five out of the 178 of the Liberal party were returned by a minority of votes. But what about the other parties? Where would they have been if some of their candidates had not got in by a minority of votes? My right hon. friend has at the present time thirty-eight followers. Of that number thirty-five were returned by a minority of votes. Almost every hon. member opposite must be thanking the lord for being of the minority on this occasion. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition would not have had as many followers as he has fingers on either hand but for those of his followers who were returned by a minority of votes.
Take the other members of the house. I hope none [DOT] of them will be offended if, for their convenience as well as ours, we speak of them combined as the independent members. They will not agree to support the government, I understand, and they do not want to support my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. Supporting outright neither the government nor the opposition, I assume that, whether they are Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or Social Credit or Reconstruction or avowedly independent, they will wish to regard themselves as independent members of the house. Unless they would deem it a mistaken way in which to speak of them all when I wish to speak of them collectively, I propose to adopt that designation throughout the session.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext: Where do you put Mr. Neill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. A. G. SLAGHT AND SECONDED BY MR. SARTO FOURNIER
speechtext:
He is in the right place just where he is; my hon. friend need not worry about him. I say that it seems proper to refer to those who avowedly support neither the government nor the opposition as the independent members of the house. They have their groups, and unfortunately or fortunately-fortunately I think-they have their differences. There are twenty-seven independent members in the house. Of that number, seventeen were returned by a minority of votes. If we take a bird's eye view of the entire situation, we find that, of the Liberal party's membership in this House of Commons 47-7 per cent were returned by a minority of votes; of the Conservative party membership, 87-5 per cent were returned by a minority of votes; and of members of independent groups, 62-9 per cent were returned by a minority of votes.
Just in case there may be any doubt in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite as to what the country thinks of the government, since it has taken office, may I say that, in the short time we have held office, there have already been three byelections. In none of these was a candidate returned by a minority of votes. In two instances, the government's candidate was returned by acclamation. In the other case, where there was an actual election to test, among other things, the views of the people of western Canada with respect to the government's wheat policy, to which my right hon. friend has referred at such length, the minister of the crown, who was opposed on the platform by a supporter in this house of my right hon. friend, and by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, was returned by a majority of between 3,000 and 4,000 votes, 3,600 in fact. Whereas the Liberal member at the last election had received only 41 per cent of the entire vote, my hon. friend the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) received 66 per cent. So far as the government is concerned, hon. members may feel that numerically we represent the people of this country in a perfectly just and fair manner. If anything, we are fewer in numbers than we would have been had there been only two parties instead of the number there were.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
